# 2 Samuel 21 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview of the Chapter

This chapter begins the "appendix" or "epilogue" of 2 Samuel (chs. 21–24), a non-chronological collection of material from David's reign arranged in a chiastic (symmetrical) structure. Chapters 21–24 contain: (A) a famine narrative (21:1–14), (B) accounts of David's warriors (21:15–22), (C) two songs of David (22:1–51; 23:1–7), (B') more warrior accounts (23:8–39), and (A') a pestilence narrative (24:1–25). (Sources: preceptaustin.org; enduringword.com; studylight.org Constable)

---

## v. 1 — The Three-Year Famine and David's Inquiry

**"During the reign of David there was a famine for three successive years, and David sought the face of the LORD."**

The phrase "sought the face of the LORD" is unique in Samuel and indicates fervent, personal inquiry. David did not assume every problem had a spiritual cause — he waited through two years before concluding this famine was more than a natural drought. Trapp observes, "The first and second year he might look upon it as a punishment laid upon them for the common sins of the land: but when he saw it continuing a third year also, he thought there was something in it more than ordinary, and therefore, although he well knew the natural cause to be drought, yet he inquired after the supernatural, as wise men should do." (enduringword.com; preceptaustin.org)

Gill notes David likely inquired "before the high priest by Urim and Thummim." The first year he may have taken no notice, hoping for a better season next year; the second year he may have begun to think of national sins; by the third year he was alarmed and feared it was on his own account. (biblehub.com/gill)

**"It is because of the blood shed by Saul and his family, because he killed the Gibeonites."**

God's answer identifies the cause as "bloodguilt" (ESV) resting on Saul and his house. The Gibeonite massacre is not recorded elsewhere in Scripture, but David does not question God. Saul's sin was not only murder but the violation of the covenant oath Joshua had sworn to the Gibeonites some 400 years earlier (Joshua 9). The whole nation was implicated because Saul acted as king — national head — and the oath was a national oath. Gleason Archer explains: "All the nation was bound by this oath for all the days to come, even though it had been obtained under false pretenses." (preceptaustin.org)

Constable suggests the famine likely occurred early in David's reign (c. 996–993 B.C.), between Mephibosheth's arrival and the Ammonite wars, partly because Rizpah would have been very old if this happened much later. (studylight.org/constable)

Ellicott answers two common questions: (1) Why was punishment delayed? Because Israel sinned and was punished as a nation, and "the lesson of the continuity of the nation's life, and of its continued responsibility from age to age, was greatly enhanced by the delay." (2) Why did it fall on David's people? Because Saul sinned as king, involving all Israel in violation of the national oath. (biblehub.com/ellicott)

---

## v. 2 — David Summons the Gibeonites

**"At this, David summoned the Gibeonites and spoke to them. (Now the Gibeonites were not Israelites, but a remnant of the Amorites. The Israelites had taken an oath concerning them, but in his zeal for Israel and Judah, Saul had sought to kill them.)"**

The parenthetical explanation identifies the Gibeonites as Amorites (an umbrella term; they were specifically Hivites per Joshua 9:7). Despite being pagan foreigners, God held Israel to the covenant made with them. Precept Austin notes this teaches that "covenant before God is still a covenant whether the two parties were Hebrews or as in this case Hebrews and pagans." (preceptaustin.org)

Saul's "zeal" here is presented not as admirable but as misguided — a cloak for pride and self-will under the guise of religious fervour. Ellicott: "His zeal in that case was of the same ungodly character with many other acts of his reign, in which pride, arrogance, and self-will were cloaked under a zeal for God's honour and His people's welfare." (biblehub.com/ellicott)

Guzik adds that this "is a good example of good intentions not excusing bad actions." (enduringword.com)

---

## v. 3 — David's Humble Approach

**"So David asked the Gibeonites, 'What shall I do for you? How can I make amends so that you may bless the inheritance of the LORD?'"**

David does not dictate terms; he comes as a servant, not a king. The word "make amends" (or "make atonement," *kāpar*) is the same technical term used in the Law for propitiatory sacrifices. Ellicott: "It means literally, to cover up, and is here used in that literal sense. David asks what he can do to so cover up the sin of Saul as to remove it from the sight of those against whom it had been committed." (biblehub.com/ellicott)

"Bless the inheritance of the LORD" means to pray for blessing on the land and people of Israel — David wanted full reconciliation, not merely appeasement. (enduringword.com; preceptaustin.org)

---

## v. 4 — The Gibeonites' Initial Reply

**"'We need no silver or gold from Saul or his house, nor should you put to death anyone in Israel for us.' 'Whatever you ask, I will do for you,' he replied."**

The Gibeonites refused monetary compensation or indiscriminate retribution. Gill: "It was not silver and gold Saul took from them, but the lives of their brethren, and therefore they insist upon life for life." This reflects the *lex talionis* principle. (biblehub.com/gill)

David's reply — "Whatever you ask, I will do" — shows total openness to making things right. (enduringword.com)

---

## vv. 5–6 — The Gibeonites' Demand

**"'As for the man who consumed us and plotted against us to exterminate us from existing within any border of Israel, let seven of his male descendants be delivered to us so that we may hang them before the LORD at Gibeah of Saul, the chosen of the LORD.' 'I will give them to you,' said the king."**

The Gibeonites name Saul ("the man who consumed us") and demand seven of his male descendants for public execution. The number seven symbolises completeness. Ellicott: "Saul being dead, his male descendants were considered as standing in his place, representing him, and responsible for his acts… The number seven is, doubtless, fixed upon as being first, a considerable and sufficient number; and then, on account of its sacred associations, and as the representative of completeness." (biblehub.com/ellicott)

"Before the LORD" indicates the execution was understood as an act of divine justice, not mere revenge. The location "Gibeah of Saul" would add public disgrace to Saul's memory. (enduringword.com; biblehub.com/gill)

Constable notes that "the Hebrew word translated 'hang' (2 Samuel 21:6) means to execute in a way that the body suffers public humiliation (cf. Numbers 25:4). Probably they suffered execution and then their bodies were hung up." (studylight.org/constable)

Gill adds that David's consent was not a violation of his oath to Saul, "for though he had sworn to Saul that he would not cut off his seed, yet as he had a divine direction in this case… this oath of his was dispensed with." (biblehub.com/gill)

---

## v. 7 — Mephibosheth Spared

**"Now the king spared Mephibosheth son of Jonathan, the son of Saul, because of the oath before the LORD between David and Jonathan son of Saul."**

David's sparing of Mephibosheth demonstrates that covenant-keeping was a two-way principle: he must satisfy the Gibeonite covenant but also honour his covenant with Jonathan. Gill observes this was "not merely or only out of affection to Mephibosheth, but because of the oath, that he might not be guilty of the same crime Saul was in slaying the Gibeonites." (biblehub.com/gill)

Constable: "David showed himself to be a true son of Yahweh by keeping his covenant with Jonathan." Saul broke Israel's covenant with the Gibeonites; David kept his covenant — a deliberate contrast. (studylight.org/constable)

---

## v. 8 — The Seven Descendants Named

**"But the king took Armoni and Mephibosheth, the two sons whom Rizpah daughter of Aiah had borne to Saul, as well as the five sons whom Merab daughter of Saul had borne to Adriel son of Barzillai the Meholathite."**

Two sons of Saul through his concubine Rizpah, and five sons of Saul's daughter Merab are handed over. (The BSB correctly reads "Merab"; the KJV/Hebrew text reads "Michal," but this is widely recognised as a scribal error, since Michal was childless — 2 Samuel 6:23 — and Merab married Adriel per 1 Samuel 18:19.) Gill explains that Merab bore the sons but Michal may have raised them after Merab's death, hence the name association. (biblehub.com/gill; studylight.org/constable)

Constable adds: "David could justly slay Saul's descendants if they had had a part in the execution of the Gibeonites. This seems to have been the case (2 Samuel 21:1; cf. Ezekiel 18:4; Ezekiel 18:20)." (studylight.org/constable)

---

## v. 9 — The Execution

**"And he delivered them into the hands of the Gibeonites, and they hanged them on the hill before the LORD. So all seven of them fell together; they were put to death in the first days of the harvest, at the beginning of the barley harvest."**

The execution took place on a hill (at Gibeah), publicly, at the start of barley harvest (mid-April, around Passover). Gill notes the Jewish tradition that it was the 16th of Nisan. The timing at Passover — commemorating Israel's liberation — was appropriate: "By getting things right with the Gibeonites, David brought Israel out from under God's oppression that Saul's sin had caused." (studylight.org/constable)

Guzik highlights the theological significance: "The method of death was also important because it fulfilled the promise of Deuteronomy 21:23: he who is hanged is accursed of God. These descendants of Saul bore the curse Saul deserved and so delivered Israel from the guilt of their sin against the Gibeonites." This foreshadows Christ bearing the curse on the cross (Galatians 3:13). (enduringword.com)

---

## v. 10 — Rizpah's Vigil

**"And Rizpah the daughter of Aiah took sackcloth and spread it out for herself on a rock. From the beginning of the harvest until the rain from heaven poured down on the bodies, she did not allow the birds of the air to rest on them by day, nor the beasts of the field by night."**

Rizpah's vigil is one of the most poignant scenes in Scripture. Gill explains she used sackcloth both as mourning attire and as a rough shelter against sun and cold. She spread it "upon the rock" — the hill where her sons hung — as a canopy for herself, not to cover the bodies. (biblehub.com/gill)

The bodies were deliberately left unburied, contravening Deuteronomy 21:22–23, because the execution was not for personal sins but to avert a national calamity; they must hang until God relented. Gill: "These men suffered not for their own personal sins, but for the sins of others, and to avert a public calamity, and therefore must hang till that was removed." (biblehub.com/gill)

How long did she watch? Ellicott estimates about six months (mid-April barley harvest to October rains). However, Gill notes Josephus's report that God sent rain immediately after the hanging, and Abarbinel thought rain came within a few days — an extraordinary summer rain like 1 Samuel 12:17. (biblehub.com/gill; biblehub.com/ellicott)

Guzik: "The coming of rain showed that the famine was over, that justice was satisfied, and that Israel was delivered." (enduringword.com)

---

## vv. 11–14a — David's Response to Rizpah and the Burial

**"When David was told what Saul's concubine Rizpah, daughter of Aiah, had done, he went and took the bones of Saul and his son Jonathan from the men of Jabesh-gilead…"**

Moved by Rizpah's devotion, David retrieves the bones of Saul and Jonathan (which the men of Jabesh-gilead had stolen from Beth-shan after the Philistines hung the bodies there — see 1 Samuel 31:8–13). Gill notes that whether Rizpah's actions were reported to David with good or ill intent is uncertain, but "it was not disagreeable to David, but served to move pity and compassion in him to the woman." (biblehub.com/gill)

David gathered the bones of the hanged seven and buried all — Saul, Jonathan, and the seven descendants — in the tomb of Saul's father Kish at Zela in Benjamin. This honourable burial demonstrated that David's actions were not motivated by personal revenge against Saul's house but by obedience to God. (enduringword.com; studylight.org/constable)

---

## v. 14b — The Famine Ends

**"After they had done everything the king had commanded, God answered their prayers for the land."**

The Hebrew reads literally "God was entreated for the land." Precept Austin explains: "We learn how God responds when people repent, humble themselves before Him, and seek Him in prayer." Note that it was not merely the execution that ended the famine; prayer (presumably David's and the nation's) also played a role. (preceptaustin.org)

Gill clarifies that God was entreated "not after the burial of the said persons, but after the seven men were hanged up; by this the wrath of God was appeased, which was seen by his sending rain and fruitful seasons." (biblehub.com/gill)

Guzik connects this to Numbers 35:33: "blood defiles the land, and no atonement can be made for the land, for the blood that is shed on it, except by the blood of him who shed it." The principle is that blood from unpunished murders defiles the land. (enduringword.com)

---

## v. 15 — David Grows Faint in Battle

**"Once again the Philistines waged war against Israel, and David and his servants went down and fought against the Philistines; but David became exhausted."**

This section (vv. 15–22) records battles with the Philistines and the defeat of four "descendants of Rapha" (giants). Constable notes these may have occurred early in David's reign or during the period of Absalom's revolt when the Philistines exploited Israel's distraction. The chronological placement is uncertain. (studylight.org/constable)

David's exhaustion marks a turning point: the great warrior is aging. Guzik: "Even a great man of God grows old. As the years went on, David became unable to fight as he once did." (enduringword.com)

---

## vv. 16–17 — Ishbi-benob and Abishai's Rescue

**"Then Ishbi-benob, a descendant of Rapha, whose bronze spear weighed three hundred shekels and who was bearing a new sword, resolved to kill David. But Abishai son of Zeruiah came to his aid, struck the Philistine, and killed him."**

Ishbi-benob was "of the sons of the giant" — a descendant of the Rephaim, the ancient giant warriors of Canaan. His spear at 300 shekels (about 7.5 lbs / 3.4 kg) was formidable but half the weight of Goliath's (1 Samuel 17:7). The "new sword" (or "new girdle," per Targum and Jarchi) may indicate a fresh commission. (biblehub.com/gill)

There is ambiguity in the Hebrew about who killed Ishbi-benob — Abishai or David. 2 Samuel 21:22 says all four fell "at the hands of David and his servants," suggesting David may have struck the final blow. But Abishai's rescue is the main point. (biblehub.com/ellicott)

**"Then David's men swore to him, 'You must never again go out with us to battle, so that the lamp of Israel may not be extinguished.'"**

"The lamp of Israel" is a rich biblical metaphor. Constable: "David, the source of Israel's human guidance, prosperity, and wellbeing — its leading light. As God was a light to His people, so the king was a source of life as His vice-regent." The figure "came to symbolize the Davidic dynasty as maintained by Yahweh (1 Kings 15:4; Psalms 132:17)." (studylight.org/constable)

Clarke: "David is considered as the lamp by which all Israel was guided, and without whom all the nation must be involved in darkness." Trapp: "The body drowneth not whilst the head is above water; when that once sinketh, death is near." (enduringword.com)

Guzik draws application: "When David's strength failed, God protected him through the strength of others. God will allow us to be in places where we need the strength of others." (enduringword.com)

---

## v. 18 — Sibbecai Kills Saph

**"Some time later at Gob, there was another battle with the Philistines. At that time Sibbecai the Hushathite killed Saph, one of the descendants of Rapha."**

Sibbecai (also called Mebunnai, 2 Samuel 23:27) was one of David's mighty men. Saph (called Sippai in 1 Chronicles 20:4) was another Rephaite giant. Gob is likely another name for Gezer (cf. 1 Chronicles 20:4). (studylight.org/constable)

This victory demonstrates that Israel could defeat giants without David on the field. (enduringword.com)

---

## v. 19 — Elhanan Kills the Brother of Goliath

**"Once again there was a battle with the Philistines at Gob, and Elhanan son of Jair the Bethlehemite killed the brother of Goliath the Gittite, the shaft of whose spear was like a weaver's beam."**

This verse has a well-known textual issue. The Hebrew of 2 Samuel 21:19 appears to say Elhanan killed Goliath, which would contradict 1 Samuel 17 (where David kills Goliath). However, 1 Chronicles 20:5 clarifies: "Elhanan son of Jair killed Lahmi the brother of Goliath the Gittite." Constable and Archer affirm the Chronicles reading as correct; the Samuel text has suffered a scribal error, omitting "the brother of." The BSB correctly supplies "the brother of." (studylight.org/constable)

The detail "the shaft of whose spear was like a weaver's beam" deliberately echoes the description of Goliath (1 Samuel 17:7), confirming this giant was of the same family line. (enduringword.com)

---

## vv. 20–21 — The Six-Fingered Giant

**"And there was still another battle at Gath, where there was a man of great stature with six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot — twenty-four in all. He too was descended from Rapha, and when he taunted Israel, Jonathan the son of David's brother Shimei killed him."**

This giant had polydactyly (six digits per extremity). Guzik notes Clarke's observation that this is a known medical phenomenon, citing a 17th-century example from Java and a personal sighting in Ireland. (enduringword.com)

Jonathan, the son of Shimei (David's brother), killed him — another victory by David's extended family and servants, not David personally. (enduringword.com)

---

## v. 22 — Summary of the Four Giants

**"So these four descendants of Rapha in Gath fell at the hands of David and his servants."**

"Descendants of Rapha" — Rapha (or the Rapha) refers to the Rephaim, the ancient giant warriors of Canaan. Guzik draws the application: "David's legacy lay not only in what he accomplished but also in what he left behind — a people prepared for victory. David's triumphs were meaningful not only for himself but for others who learned victory through his teaching and example." (enduringword.com)

G. Campbell Morgan (cited by Guzik): "Let those who after long service find themselves waning in strength, be content to abide with the people of God, still shining for them as a lamp, and thus enabling them to carry on the same Divine enterprises." (enduringword.com)

## Points of Difference Among Protestant Traditions

*Specific tradition-by-tradition differences on this chapter proved difficult to locate from the approved source list. However, several notable differences emerged from the sources consulted:*

**On the morality of the execution of Saul's descendants:**
- **Gill (Reformed Baptist / older evangelical):** Defends the execution as just and consistent with divine direction. The ceremonial law (requiring burial the same day in Deut. 21:22–23) gave way to the moral necessity of publicly sanctifying God's name. He cites the rabbinic principle: "It is better that one letter should be rooted out of the law, than that the name of God should not be sanctified openly." (biblehub.com/gill)
- **Guzik / Enduring Word (Pentecostal/Charismatic):** Emphasises the typological dimension — the hanging prefigures Christ bearing the curse on the cross, making the passage primarily Christological. (enduringword.com)
- **Ellicott (Anglican):** Takes a more historical-critical approach, explaining the ancient Near Eastern concepts of corporate guilt and representative justice as the framework for understanding the text, without offering strong moral defence or condemnation. (biblehub.com/ellicott)
- **Constable (Dallas Seminary / Evangelical):** Suggests the descendants likely participated in the massacre themselves, which would make the execution consistent with Ezekiel 18:4, 20 (individual responsibility). (studylight.org/constable)

**On the chapter's placement (chronology debate):**
- Some (Gill, citing Jewish sources) place this early in David's reign, perhaps within a year of Saul's death.
- Constable dates it c. 996–993 B.C., between Mephibosheth's arrival and the Ammonite wars.
- Others (like Ellicott) note the phrase "in the days of David" is "purposely indefinite." (biblehub.com/ellicott)

**Catholic and Orthodox readings:** Specific Catholic or Orthodox commentary on 2 Samuel 21 was not locatable through the approved sources (newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org) within the search constraints. The standard Catholic approach would likely be found in the works of St. Augustine or the *Catena Aurea*, though 2 Samuel is not covered in the latter.

**Modern scholarship (netbible.org, bibleodyssey.org):** Not retrievable within the search limits.

**Debated popular modern teaching (prosperity, word of faith, hyper-grace):** No specific teachings on this chapter from these movements were locatable through the approved sources.
